metadata.title: Evansville, Indiana — electric railways
metadata.note: The interurbans radiating from Evansville, and the Evansville Suburban and Newburgh that they ran into town over. Companion to evansville_hub.geojson, which holds the steam roads.
metadata.geometry_method: ROAD-GRID APPROXIMATION THROUGHOUT. Unlike the steam layer, none of these lines survive in OpenStreetMap under any railway tag — a full-tag sweep of the Evansville area found no traction, tram or interurban geometry at all. Each line is therefore drawn along the modern road corridor it is documented to have followed, and checked against its documented mileage: 10.1 mi vs 11 (ES&N), 31.8 vs 31 (E&E), 30.1 vs 28 (Princeton), 21.6 vs 20 (Mount Vernon). Treat every alignment here as indicative, not surveyed.
metadata.horsecar_audit: Rule 5 check. Evansville’s street railway was organised the year after the Civil War for mule-drawn cars and none of those years are drawn anywhere in this repo. The ES&N is drawn from 1889, when it opened under steam; every other feature here was electric from the day it opened.
metadata.freight_only_audit: Rule 1 check. The ES&N is drawn to 1930, when its passenger service ended, not to the 1948 abandonment — it hauled only freight in between, and its note says so without drawing it.
metadata.interurban_audit: Rule 7: every electric feature here links separate communities — Evansville to Newburgh, Rockport, Mount Vernon and Princeton — so all are tagged interurban and draw dashed. The ES&N’s pre-1905 steam years are tagged intercity_rail instead, since it was not yet an electric railway.
not_yet_sourced: The Evansville city streetcar system (electrified 1892, last car 1 February 1939) is NOT DRAWN. Its lines ran on city streets and a street-by-street route list was not obtained — only two routes surfaced (West Heights: Fulton–Franklin–Barker–Broadway, 3.75 mi; Oak Summit: Fulton–Franklin–Mt Vernon Ave–Harmony Way). Drawing two of a dozen-odd routes would misrepresent the system, so none are drawn.

The Evansville, Henderson and Owensboro Railway (1912–1928) is NOT DRAWN. Its Evansville–Henderson link was a steel ferry across the Ohio rather than a rail crossing, and a road-grid trace of its Kentucky rail portion failed to route.
Who operated the Evansville–Princeton interurban after 1906.
Every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh here is an estimate; no interurban timetable was consulted.

properties.line: Evansville Suburban and Newburgh: Evansville – Newburgh
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATED, NOT TRACED FROM THE RAILWAY. No part of this line survives in OpenStreetMap, so the route is drawn along the modern road corridor the interurban is documented to have connected — it shows where the line went, not the exact right of way, and departs from it wherever the road was later realigned. Drawn Evansville–Newburgh along the Covert Avenue / IN-662 corridor: 10.1 mi against a documented 11 mi.
properties.speed_source: Estimated. Interurban schedules for these lines were not consulted; 30–35 km/h is a typical average for an Indiana interurban with frequent stops.

segments.note: Chartered December 1887 and open to Newburgh within a few years, worked by steam. Drawn as a steam railroad for these years and as an interurban from 1905, when the line was electrified — the two features share the same geometry. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1887 charter, 1905 electrification, 1930 end of passenger service, 1948 abandonment.

segments.note: Electrified in 1905 and run as an 11-mile interurban. Passenger service ended in 1930 as highways took the traffic; the company carried freight only until the mines closed, and the route was abandoned in May 1948 — those later years are deliberately not drawn (Rule 1). Evansville & Eastern cars kept running over this track to Evansville until 1938, which is drawn as a separate feature. Headway estimated.

properties.line: Evansville and Eastern Electric: Evansville – Rockport
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATED, NOT TRACED FROM THE RAILWAY. No part of this line survives in OpenStreetMap, so the route is drawn along the modern road corridor the interurban is documented to have connected — it shows where the line went, not the exact right of way, and departs from it wherever the road was later realigned. Drawn Evansville–Newburgh–Yankeetown–Hatfield–Rockport along IN-662 and IN-66: 31.8 mi against a documented 31 mi Evansville–Rockport (21 mi of it the company’s own Newburgh–Rockport main). The 3-mile Richland spur is not drawn.
properties.speed_source: Estimated. Interurban schedules for these lines were not consulted; 30–35 km/h is a typical average for an Indiana interurban with frequent stops.

segments.note: Opened 10 June 1906. The company’s own line was the 21 miles Newburgh–Rockport, through Yankeetown and Hatfield; a traffic agreement let its cars run the rest of the way into Evansville over the Evansville Suburban and Newburgh, making a 31-mile electric route against 51 miles by steam. One of the very few American electric lines that paralleled no steam railroad. Consolidated into the Evansville and Ohio Valley in 1918. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 10 June 1906 opening, 21-mile Newburgh–Rockport main, through cars to Evansville over the ES&N, and the 17 October 1938 abandonment of the Rockport line.

segments.note: Interurban north from Evansville through Haubstadt and Fort Branch to Princeton, opened 1903 and abandoned in 1933. It was not part of the 1918 Evansville and Ohio Valley consolidation, and who ran it after 1906 is not established here — see metadata.not_yet_sourced. Headway estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1903 opening and 1933 abandonment come from Historic Evansville’s line list, but the operating company after 1906 was not checked, so this feature carries the original builder’s name for its whole span — which may be wrong for the later years.
